source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste, Linzen (2024) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models (NAACL)
finding: PaLM 2 models answer syllogisms more accurately than people and share many human biases (figural effect, the same top syllogistic fallacies). Larger models fit an mReasoner 'deliberative' profile better. But models almost never say 'nothing follows', where people at least sometimes do.
numbers: Human data: Ragni et al. 2019, 139 people, 27 syllogisms, 9 answer options. Human accuracy about 50%. Best LM about 75%; scale did not raise accuracy steadily. On the 37 syllogisms whose only correct answer is 'nothing follows', model accuracy is near 0%. 1,296 mReasoner settings (923 finished); one principal component carries 77% of mReasoner variance and loads on the System-2 (counterexample search) and WEAKEN parameters. With correct answers zeroed out, larger models still look more System-2 (PC1 correlation 0.6 with SYSTM2). Llama 2 is about human-level overall but fails easy syllogisms that people solve.
quote: LMs rarely produce the response 'nothing follows', even for the 37 syllogisms for which this is the correct conclusion
limits: Zero-shot chain of thought only; the 'nothing follows' failure is worst under this prompt, and a different scoring method can elicit it. Syllogisms only. The mReasoner fit is a behavioural match, not proof of the same mechanism.
agent_relevance: Confirms the counterexample step is the weak spot: the model stops at the first model and does not search for a second one. Our schema needs a forced 'try to build a model where the premises hold and the conclusion fails' step with an explicit 'nothing follows' exit.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and Modal Reasoning in Large Language Models (EMNLP)
finding: 29 LLMs were tested on single-step inferences with 'if' and 'might/must'. All made basic mistakes. Even the best accepted invalid modal patterns and contradicted themselves across related inferences. Zero-shot chain of thought helped a lot; few-shot did not.
numbers: 20 items per pattern; yes/no answers; temperature 0 and 1. Zero-shot accuracy on the uncontroversial patterns ranged 45% to 89.5% (chance 50%). Zero-shot CoT gain per model: +0.2 to +21.5 points; the best models reached about 90%. Few-shot gain ranged -8 to +12.5, mixed. Nearly all models accepted two clearly invalid modal inferences (must(A or B) therefore must A or must B; might A and might B therefore might (A and B)). The best models judged the contested conditional pattern CMP valid under zero-shot, against human judgment.
quote: all models commit basic fallacies in reasoning with modals and conditionals
limits: Logic-style framing, not the Johnson-Laird illusion materials. No human data collected in this paper; human judgments come from the literature.
agent_relevance: Possibility words (might, must) are an error zone even for strong models. For modal premises, have the agent first list the possibilities each premise allows, then check the conclusion against that list, and use step-by-step reasoning (cheap, clear gain).

source: Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Abe, Mineshima, Okada (2024) Exploring Reasoning Biases in LLMs Through Syllogism: NeuBAROCO
finding: Bilingual (English, Japanese) syllogism set from psychology experiments. LLMs show human-like belief bias, conversion errors and atmosphere effects. Hardest items are the 'neither entailed nor contradicted' ones. Translating to logic is nearly perfect, but the reasoning step still fails.
numbers: 790 NLI items (entail, contradict, neutral), 80-95 multiple-choice items, 90 items in Translate-and-Explain. 13B models 20-30% (chance) on multiple choice; 70B and GPT models 42% to 95%; human overall 53% in the Japanese set. GPT-4 scored about 30 points lower on neutral items than on others. Accuracy lower for belief-incongruent items and for conversion/atmosphere-labelled items. GPT-4 translation to predicate logic: 87/90 English, 86/90 Japanese; to set theory 82/90 and 69/90. GPT-3.5 Japanese to set theory only 28/90.
limits: Human comparison is loose (different samples and formats). The multiple-choice version has no 'none of them' answer, so it flatters the models.
agent_relevance: Reading the premises is not the bottleneck; drawing the conclusion is. Model-building must target the inference step, and 'neither' (open possibility) must be a legitimate output.

source: Ando, Morishita, Abe, Mineshima, Okada (2023) Evaluating Large Language Models with NeuBAROCO: Syllogistic Reasoning Ability and Human-like Biases
finding: Earlier, smaller version of the NeuBAROCO study; zero-shot GPT-3.5 on NLI syllogisms, reports human-like biases.
numbers: 375 NLI tasks, zero-shot GPT-3.5 only (as described by Ozeki et al. 2024; this paper was downloaded but not read in full).
limits: Superseded by Ozeki et al. 2024. Not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Low; use the 2024 version.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, Sheahan, Creswell, Kumaran, McClelland, Hill (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks (PNAS Nexus)
finding: On natural language inference, syllogism validity and the Wason task, LMs and people both reason better when the content fits belief. Models also show the human link between answer confidence and response time. Content effect is stronger on harder tasks; the instruction prompt mattered little.
numbers: Models: Chinchilla 70B, PaLM 2-M and -L, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5, plus human participants on matched online tasks. Wason: realistic rules beat arbitrary rules in humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L and GPT-3.5 (all z > 2.2). Humans did not beat chance overall on the Wason task. Without the instruction prompt results were similar, except Chinchilla on belief-violating NLI items; PaLM 2-L over 75% in every Wason condition in one setting.
limits: Tasks are NLI, syllogism, Wason; not model-theory illusions. Human sample modest; human Wason accuracy low.
agent_relevance: Content pulls the model off the form. Add a step that restates the argument with abstract or swapped labels and re-checks it (guards against belief bias).

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A Systematic Analysis of LLMs as Soft Reasoners: The Case of Syllogistic Inferences (EMNLP)
finding: Compared zero-shot chain of thought, in-context examples (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Pythia and LLaMA. ICL did not teach the models to say 'nothing follows', even when the examples had the same schema. SFT did, and removed the content bias. Errors fit the Atmosphere heuristic.
numbers: Human reference (Khemlani and Johnson-Laird 2012): 44.63% on valid syllogisms, 40.97% on invalid. LLaMA-3 70B: 58.89% on valid, correlation 0.80 with human difficulty ordering. Atmosphere theory predicts 92% of LLaMA zero-shot CoT correct valid conclusions and 82.97% (invalid) / 62.79% (valid) of its errors. SFT models near ceiling and nearly no contradictory answers (0.31%); ICL made models more self-contradictory. Multi-premise (2,3,4 premises, pseudo-words, 280 points): zero-shot CoT worse with more premises; SFT dropped more than ICL but stayed higher. Instruction tuning helped invalid items but hurt valid ones.
limits: Small and mid-size open models (Pythia 1.4B, LLaMA-3 8B for the learning-strategy table). SFT is training, which our agent will not do.
agent_relevance: A prompt with worked examples is not enough to make the model give up on a conclusion. A structural check (a model-building step that must either succeed or end in 'nothing follows') is likelier to work than examples.

source: Koralus and Wang-Masciantica (2023) Humans in Humans Out: On GPT Converging Toward Common Sense in both Success and Failure
finding: The only study found that put illusory inferences of the model-theory type (disjunction plus a categorical premise) to GPT. GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 gave human-style fallacies, and more of them as models grew. Example: 'Either Jane is kneeling by the fire and she is looking at the TV, or else Mark is standing at the window and he is peering into the garden. Jane is kneeling by the fire.' GPT-4 concluded that Jane is looking at the TV (the human illusion). Order effect: the fallacy appeared for 'ace and queen, or king and ten. There is a king' but not when the king premise came first.
numbers: ETR61 benchmark: 61 problems (Wason card task, illusory inferences, decoy effect, opportunity-cost neglect and others). Output matched ETR-predicted answers: GPT-3 59%, GPT-3.5 77%, GPT-4 75%. Human-like fallacious outputs: 18% (GPT-3), 33% (GPT-3.5), 34% (GPT-4). Correct inference rates 49%, 61%, 72%. Each question asked in a fresh context; GPT-3 at temperature 0.7.
quote: the production of human-like fallacious judgments increased from 18% in GPT-3 to 33% in GPT-3.5 and 34% in GPT-4
limits: The authors' frame is the Erotetic Theory of Reason (ETR), not mental models theory, though the illusory items overlap with Johnson-Laird's. Chat interface, March 2023, single sample per item, small N per subtype; the illusory items are only part of the 61.
agent_relevance: Better models can be MORE prone to the human illusion. Evidence that a Principle-of-Truth guardrail is needed: after reading a disjunction, list what is false in each alternative before using a later premise.

source: Koralus and Wang-Masciantica (2023) same paper, Study 2: erotetic prompt versus plain step-by-step prompt
finding: A prompt that says: list the premises, turn each into a question, keep the alternatives, then reason step by step. It blocked fallacies far better than plain 'reason step by step' for GPT-3.5, and no better for GPT-4 or GPT-3.
numbers: Fallacies blocked: GPT-3.5: control step-by-step prompt 4/17 versus erotetic prompt 14/17 (p = 0.0045). GPT-4: 8/19 versus 7/19 (p = 0.77). GPT-3: 4/8 versus 4/8. Only prompts that had earlier produced the predicted fallacy were retested.
quote: turn each premise into a question to make a new list of questions; treat questions as possible alternatives
limits: Tiny counts; only previously failed items retested; no replication; GPT-4 saw no gain. Blocking a fallacy does not prove the right answer.
agent_relevance: A short 'keep every alternative open' procedure can beat generic step-by-step on a weaker model. For strong models the gain may vanish, so test it in our harness before trusting it.

source: Chan, Gaizauskas, Zhao (2025) RULEBREAKERS: Challenging LLMs at the Crossroads between Formal Logic and Human-like Reasoning (ICML)
finding: Pairs of arguments with the same logical form: in one the conclusion is acceptable, in the other (a 'rulebreaker') world knowledge makes it wrong (adapted from Johnson-Laird 1983: 'Anne is in Stockholm or somewhere in Sweden. Anne is not in Sweden'). Models apply the rule too rigidly. Logic-tool pipelines made it worse.
numbers: 7 LLMs; paired accuracy (both items right), chance 0.25; only Llama-3-8B-Instruct above 0.6. GPT-4o, Gemma-2-27b and Phi-3-mini were perfect or near-perfect on ordinary items but worst on rulebreakers; GPT-4o scored 0.0022 on one subset. Prompt rewording plus premise prefixes raised paired accuracy by up to +24.13 points (gemma-2-27b), but all models stayed between 31.27 and 69.12. gpt-3.5-turbo: LogicLM and SymbolicCoT raised ordinary-item accuracy but lowered rulebreaker accuracy; chain of thought made the same trade, less severely. A Llama-3.1-8B fine-tuned on propositional logic did better on ordinary items and worse on rulebreakers.
limits: Only two rules (modus tollens, disjunctive syllogism); entities are countries/cities and categories. Phrasing sensitivity: Llama-3-8B paired accuracy varied by over 0.4 across phrasings.
agent_relevance: Do not bolt formal logic onto the loop and call it done: it increases rigidity. The model-theory view (meaning and knowledge shape the possibilities) is the right guard; the agent should ask 'what do I know that makes this possibility impossible?' before applying a form.

source: Wang, Yin, Zhang, et al. (2025/2026) MindCube: Spatial Mental Modeling from Limited Views
finding: Vision-language models are near chance at building a mental model of a room from a few views. Giving a ready-made cognitive map hurt. Prompting the model to write its own map, then reason over it, helped a little when frozen and a lot after training. Self-built structure plus free reasoning beats either alone.
numbers: 21,154 questions, 3,268 images. Raw answer-only baseline 37.81% (Qwen2.5-VL-3B, MindCube-Tiny). Extra interpolated view: no gain (-0.09). Pre-computed map as input: 32.00% (worse). Free-form reasoning alone: 40.48%; with its own map before reasoning: 41.43%. Generated maps similar to ground truth under 50%. Fine-tuned map-then-reason: 57.8% (+20.0). Plus reinforcement learning: 61.3% (+23.5). RL from scratch: 49.52%. Best off-the-shelf model, DeepSeek-VL2-Small: 47.62%.
limits: Images, not text. Large gains come from training, not prompting. Tiny model for the ablations.
agent_relevance: For spatial tasks, the model should construct its own explicit layout (grid or table) and then reason from it; an externally given structure it did not build does not help. Frozen-prompt gain is small, so expect modest benefit from the schema alone.

source: Jiang, Qin, Li (2026) SpatialText: A Pure-Text Cognitive Benchmark for Spatial Understanding in LLMs
finding: Text-only spatial benchmark built to test whether models hold a viewpoint-free spatial model. Fact retrieval and fixed-frame (allocentric) reasoning are good. Switching to the observer's viewpoint (egocentric) falls to near random.
numbers: Overall accuracy: DeepSeek-V3.2 0.81, Qwen-Flash 0.75, OpenPangu-7B 0.71. Basic retrieval: most models above 0.85, DeepSeek-V3.2 0.91. Physical-constraint items: Qwen-Flash 0.79, DeepSeek-V3.2 0.74, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B 0.37. Dynamic items: OpenPangu 0.72, Qwen-Flash 0.69, DeepSeek-V3.2 0.77. Egocentric perspective transformation near chance; 'bed-north' error when a person lies with head to the north.
limits: Mostly 7B-8B open models plus DeepSeek-V3.2; no frontier closed model in the numbers I read. Preprint; sample sizes per task not checked.
agent_relevance: When a task changes the point of view, the agent must write the frame explicitly (who faces where, what is left of what) and then recompute, not trust the story. Add a reference-frame check to the spatial route.

source: Wu, Mao, Zhang, Xia, Dong, Cui, Wei (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning (NeurIPS)
finding: Asking GPT-4 to draw the state after each step (ASCII grid) improves multi-step spatial reasoning over plain chain of thought and over a vision model given images. It does not help when plain arithmetic suffices.
numbers: Natural-language navigation: GPT-4 with VoT beats GPT-4 with visualization disabled by 23.5 points; versus CoT only p < 0.16. Complete visual tracking: 87.1% of VoT outputs versus 57.4% of CoT outputs. Ring navigation (200 instances, ring size 12): CoT 52.5% beats VoT 49.5%. Smaller models tested (GPT-3.5, Llama3-8B, Llama3-70B): VoT beat CoT in most tasks for Llama3-70B except visual tiling.
limits: Grid worlds only. Visualisations are often wrong. The main results table was scrambled in my text extraction; I used numbers stated in the text.
agent_relevance: Closest published analogue to 'build an iconic model and update it': write the state after every step. Use it for layout and navigation; skip when the task reduces to arithmetic.

source: Chen, Chi, Wang, Zhou (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models (ICML)
finding: Shuffling the order of premises, with the content unchanged, cuts logic accuracy; the best order matches the order of the proof. Parallels the human figural and continuity effects in model theory, where an easier-to-integrate premise order helps.
numbers: Abstract: permuting premise order can cause a drop of over 30% across tested models (GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo, PaLM 2-L, Gemini 1.0 Pro). New math benchmark R-GSM also shows a large drop.
limits: Rule-chain deduction, not model-theory tasks; I read the abstract and method text but did not verify every table.
agent_relevance: Re-order premises into a chain (A-B, B-C) before building a model. Cheap, input-side step. Add as a normalisation operator.

source: Seals and Shalin (2024) Evaluating the Deductive Competence of Large Language Models (NAACL)
finding: Wason selection task, several LLMs: weak in the usual form. Changing format and content did not lift overall performance, and the interactions did not match human ones. The human content effect (social rules easy) was much weaker in models.
numbers: Humans solve social-rule versions about 70% of the time (Griggs and Cox 1982); LLMs about 30% with domain-conditional scoring. Chance is 1/6.
limits: Older open models, probability scoring rather than generation, no chain of thought.
agent_relevance: Modest. Format tricks are not the lever; process steps are. Human-like content effects are not a safe prediction for models.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models (Royal Society Open Science)
finding: Seven models on classic cognitive-psychology tasks (including the Wason task). Models are irrational, but not in the human way: wrong answers are often not human-like, and the same prompt gives different answers on different runs.
numbers: 7 LLMs; responses coded on two axes (correct, human-like). A facilitated Wason version is included. Exact per-model rates not extracted in my read.
limits: Qualitative coding by the authors; I did not extract per-task percentages.
agent_relevance: Expect inconsistency across samples; sample several times and compare the possibility sets, not just the final answers.

source: Abe, Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Mineshima, Okada (2026) Evaluation of Deontic Conditional Reasoning in LLMs: The Case of Wason's Selection Task
finding: Models reason better with rules of permission and duty than with descriptive rules, like people, and their errors look like matching bias (choosing cards that mention items in the rule).
numbers: Accuracy higher on deontic than descriptive rules for all models and prompt types, gains from +5.0 to +41.2 points. Zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought compared; exact per-model cells not extracted.
limits: Matching bias is also what a model that copies words would do; not proof of a human-like process.
agent_relevance: Reframing a falsification task as a concrete rule-check (who could break the rule?) may help. Use as a rewrite operator for abstract conditional tasks.

source: Tsvilodub, Marty, Ramotowska, Romoli, Franke (2024) Experimental Pragmatics with Machines: Testing LLM Predictions for the Inferences of Plain and Embedded Disjunctions (CogSci)
finding: Possibility inferences from 'or' (the speaker thinks each disjunct is possible; free choice) tested on LLMs with the same paradigm as human studies. The best models align with human differences between inferences, but not uniformly, and many models do worse than people on control items.
numbers: Models: GPT-3.5, Llama-2 (7B, 13B, 70B), Mistral-7B, Mixtral, Pythia. Control accuracy (three studies): human 0.89/0.95/0.94; GPT-3.5 0.94/0.72/0.76; Llama-2-70b 0.69/0.90/0.86; Mistral-Instruct 0.54/0.64/0.75. Fit to human acceptance rates: GPT-3.5 highest, Llama-2-70b close; not perfect.
limits: Pragmatics, not deduction. Pre-2024 models. Visual boxes were turned into text.
agent_relevance: 'A or B' tends to be read as 'both possible'. This is the same default model theory predicts. The agent can use it, but must flag when a disjunction is exclusive versus inclusive.

source: Guan, He, Zheng, Chen, Zhang, Yu (2024) Towards Generalist Prompting for LLMs by Mental Models (MeMo)
finding: A prompt that defines 'mental models' (Munger-style thinking tools, not Johnson-Laird's possibility models) and lets the model choose which to apply. Matches or beats other zero-shot prompts on logic and STEM. Warning: it shares the name only, not the theory.
numbers: StrategyQA GPT-4: +6.0 points over direct query. Cause-and-Effect: +4.6; Figure of Speech: +10.2 (GPT-3.5 over direct query). On FOLIO the most-chosen mental models were logical and deductive reasoning. Ablation: both the definition and the examples add gain.
limits: Different meaning of 'mental model'; long prompt, high token cost; no model-theory test.
agent_relevance: Do not cite this as support for Johnson-Laird's method. It does suggest that a menu-of-strategies prompt (select a thinking tool per task) is a cheap, general gain.

source: Dong, Jamnik, Lio (2025) Sphere Neural-Networks for Rational Reasoning (v4)
finding: A neural system that decides syllogisms by building and inspecting an Euler-diagram model, and builds a counter-model for every invalid one. This is mental-model-style model construction in a neural net. It is perfect on long chains where ChatGPT degrades.
numbers: Exp 10.1: all 24 valid syllogisms among 256 found; a counter-example built for every invalid one. Exp 10.2: 240 valid of 1,200 long-chained candidates (3 to 12 terms) all found. gpt-3.5-turbo best 80% (3 terms) falling to 51.67% at 12 terms; gpt-4o 95.83% best, 89.17% at long chains. SphNN 100%, needs up to about 2 minutes at 12 terms.
limits: Syllogisms only; the authors' own architecture; time cost grows with chain length.
agent_relevance: A model-building checker outside the LLM is possible and exact for small domains. For our agent: a tool step (code, set operations) that builds all models for quantified premises could replace LLM intuition.

source: Dong, Jamnik, Lio (2025) Sphere Neural-Networks, Experiment 10.3: the neural checker as System 2 giving feedback to ChatGPT
finding: A model-building checker sent feedback to ChatGPT ('this answer is not correct') for up to 10 rounds. Accuracy rose a little. ChatGPT often ignored the feedback.
numbers: 256 atomic syllogism satisfiability tasks. gpt-3.5-turbo: 47.27% to 56.64% (121 right with no feedback; 145 with feedback; irrationality ratio 48.05% to 40.23%). gpt-4o: 77.39% to 80.01% (irrationality 21.48% to 17.19%). 111 (gpt-3.5) and 51 (gpt-4o) tasks still needed all 10 feedback rounds.
limits: Only 'wrong' feedback, no hint of a correct model; tasks are simple. Gains small.
agent_relevance: Bare 'you are wrong' feedback is weak. If a checker finds a counterexample, feed back the concrete counter-model, not just a verdict.

source: Kargupta et al. (2025) Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
finding: 192K reasoning traces from 18 models plus 54 human think-aloud traces, coded for 28 cognitive elements. Models use few of the elements that predict success on ill-structured problems and fall back to rigid forward steps. A prompt that scaffolds the successful structure helps capable models and hurts weak ones.
numbers: Meta-analysis of 1,600 LLM-reasoning papers: sequential organization 55%, decomposition 60%, self-awareness 16%. Test-time guidance: up to +66.7% on some ill-structured problem types (Qwen3 family and larger R1-Distill); losses over 50% (up to -72.0%) for small models such as Hermes-3-Llama-3-8B and DeepScaleR-1.5B. About 50 problems per type.
limits: Small samples per cell (about 50); wide variance; the taxonomy is not specific to mental models.
agent_relevance: A scaffold is not free: strong models profit, small ones can break. Our agent should gate heavy scaffolding on model strength and check the baseline each time.

source: Joishy, Balappanawar, Bonagiri, Gaur, Thirunarayan, Kumaraguru (2026) Flying Pigs, FaR and Beyond: Evaluating LLM Reasoning in Counterfactual Worlds
finding: When premises contradict world knowledge (a counterfactual world), accuracy drops. A single instruction to first flag any clash between the premises and what the model knows narrows the gap.
numbers: 11 LLMs, six datasets, new CounterLogic benchmark (9 schemas, 1 to 9 steps, half valid and half invalid, half belief-aligned and half conflicting). Average drop in counterfactual scenarios: 14%. Flag-and-Reason: gap reduced to 7%, overall accuracy +4%.
limits: Counterfactual here means premises false in the real world, not Byrne's 'if only' thought about alternatives to a real event.
agent_relevance: Cheap guardrail: 'name anything in the premises that clashes with what you believe, then reason only from the premises'.

source: Jha, Jha, Lincoln, Bastian, Velasquez, Ewetz, Neema (2023) Neuro Symbolic Reasoning for Planning: Counterexample Guided Inductive Synthesis Using LLMs and SAT Solving
finding: An agent loop where an LLM proposes a plan and a solver returns a concrete counterexample, which goes back to the model as the next prompt. Counterexample-in-the-loop is a working LLM-agent pattern, though not mental-models theory by name.
numbers: Blocks-world planning, 20 random problems per size. GPT-4 alone solved 19 of 20 problems at 3 blocks and 2 of 20 at 10 blocks (as read in the text). Iterations of counterexample feedback counted for 3, 4, 5 and 6 blocks for GPT-4 and GPT-3.5.
limits: The solver gives the counterexample, not the LLM. Blocks world only. I did not extract the full iteration table.
agent_relevance: The strongest working model of a counterexample operator: the useful part is the concrete failing case. If the agent has code execution, use it as the counterexample generator.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2019) Why Machines Don't (yet) Reason Like People (KI - Kunstliche Intelligenz 33)
finding: Argues that theorem provers and nonmonotonic logics cannot match human reasoning, because people reason over possibilities, not proofs from logical form. Describes working computational systems based on iconic possibilities that mimic human inferences and errors.
numbers: Fig. 1 compares a possibility-based simulation with Hinterecker et al. (2016) data for modal conclusions from non-modal premises (Exp 1 and Exp 3); the fit is described as close but no correlation is quoted. Example the paper says people accept: 'It rained or it is hot, or both' therefore 'possibly it rained and it is hot' (invalid in every standard modal logic).
limits: Position paper; written before LLMs reasoned at the current level (the deep-learning discussion is brief and pre-GPT).
agent_relevance: Gives the design rule: compute with a small set of possibilities; restrict to one possibility to mimic fast error, expand to all to approach logic. Maps onto a single-model draft state followed by an expansion state.

source: Ragni, Brand, Riesterer (2021) The Predictive Power of Spatial Relational Reasoning Models: A New Evaluation Approach (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Re-implemented and compared mental-model computer systems for spatial reasoning (PRISM, SpatialReasoner variants, VerbalReasoner) by how well they predict each individual's answers. On easy problems they all just reproduce logic; they only differ where people deviate from logic.
numbers: Four datasets: 33, 30, 49 and 51 participants. Upper bound (best-of-models 'optimal') about 88% (figural data), 76% (continuity), 82% (preference), 100% (small-large scale). Best single models: SpatialReasoner-adapted 76% on continuity (others 75%, transitive-closure baseline 75%); preference data: PRISM and VerbalReasoner 71.9% (SpatialReasoner-initial 57.1%); small-large scale: PRISM, SpatialReasoner-adapted and -credulous 79.1% (transitive closure 73.4%). Median predictive power about 80% across datasets.
limits: Mechanical Turk data, small samples; models barely beat plain logic baselines on the easy datasets.
agent_relevance: A mental-model scaffold only adds value where the problem is indeterminate. For determinate chains, plain deduction is as good; save heavy model-building for ambiguous cases (cost-aware routing).

source: Khemlani et al. mReasoner v0.9 (modeltheory.org page and GitHub skhemlani/mReasoner); Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2022) Reasoning about properties: a computational theory (Psychological Review)
finding: mReasoner is the unified computer implementation of the model theory: it builds a small iconic model from the premises, scans it for a conclusion, and (if a System-2 step runs) searches for counterexamples and revises. Four parameters (model length LEN, BROAD, System-2 probability SYSTM2, WEAKEN) set how it behaves. Code is public (LISP, Mac binary 2017).
numbers: Web page read: version 0.9.6188, last updated 2017-06-28. In Eisape et al. (2024), 1,296 parameter settings were run (100 runs per syllogism each); one component explains 77% of variance. The Psychological Review article itself was not opened.
limits: The page lists no fit numbers; the Psychological Review paper was not opened. It has no belief or knowledge handling (stated in a secondary source).
agent_relevance: Its four knobs are a ready-made design vocabulary for the schema: how many tokens in a model, how broad, how often to search for counterexamples, whether to weaken to a safer conclusion.

source: Gu, Dalvi Mishra, Clark (2023) Do language models have coherent mental models of everyday things? (ACL)
finding: Probes of 100 everyday things (parts and relations) show GPT-3 and Macaw hold fragments but not a coherent part-whole picture. A constraint layer on top of the LM raises accuracy and removes contradictions.
numbers: 11,720 true/false questions; accuracy 54-59%; 19-43% conditional constraint violations; with a constraint satisfaction layer accuracy up 16-20 points.
limits: 'Mental model' here means world knowledge, not possibility models; models are 2022 vintage. Only the abstract and introduction were read.
agent_relevance: External consistency constraints (symmetry, transitivity) repair incoherent answers. For relational reasoning, a checker that applies those constraints is cheap and helpful.

source: Nighojkar, Moydinboyev, Duong, Licato (2025) Giving AI Personalities Leads to More Human-Like Reasoning
finding: Abstract read only: persona prompts plus a genetic search over weights let LLMs match the spread of human answers on fast (System 1) and slow (System 2) NLI items; Llama and Mistral beat GPT models.
numbers: Not extracted (abstract only).
limits: Only the abstract was read.
agent_relevance: Low. Varied prompts change the answer distribution; useful only if we want to imitate people, not to be correct.
